name: Freedom 7 / MR-3
dispatch: Freedom 7 is where American human spaceflight begins. Three weeks after Gagarin had already orbited the Earth, Alan Shepard's flight was shorter, lower, and slower — fifteen minutes, straight up and straight back down, never even reaching orbit — and the country celebrated anyway, because for the first time an American had left the planet. What set it apart from Gagarin's flight was the man: Shepard hand-flew his capsule's attitude in space, where Gagarin had ridden a fully automated one, and to a program built around test pilots that difference was everything. Twenty days later, its success gave Kennedy the nerve to stand before Congress and bet the nation on the Moon. A small flight that started something very large.
description: Alan Shepard's 15-minute suborbital flight — first American in space, 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's Vostok 1 orbital flight. Apogee 187 km; max-g 11.6 g during re-entry; max-Q 3.7 g. Capsule Freedom 7 splashed down 487 km downrange in the Atlantic. Shepard reportedly remarked "What a beautiful view" at apogee. The flight was suborbital because the Mercury-Redstone launcher couldn't reach orbital velocity; subsequent orbital Mercury missions used the more powerful Atlas LV-3B. Capsule Freedom 7 is on display at the JFK Presidential Library, Boston MA.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Mercury-Redstone 3 (MR-3) from Cape Canaveral LC-5 1961-05-05 14:34 UTC.

events.label: APOGEE
events.note: Apogee 187 km after 2.5 minutes; weightlessness for ~5 min.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Capsule splashed down 487 km downrange in Atlantic Ocean. Recovery by USS Lake Champlain.
